title: The Blind Road: Folklore as Cover Story
body:
British werewolf stories tend to stay on the moors. Blackout Moon asks what happens when the moors report to Whitehall — when the folklore is the cover, and the paperwork is the monster. A conspiracy thriller with claws, set in a country that files everything.

The trilogy runs from Blackout Moon through Silent Frequency to The Red Threshold, each book widening the circle of who knew.

title: Writing a Conspiracy Without Losing the Reader
body:
Conspiracy plots collapse under their own paperwork if the reader cannot track who wants what. My rule is one protagonist question per book, answered by the last page, with the larger machine only glimpsed. The reader should finish knowing more and trusting less.

Paranoia is a mood the prose has to earn scene by scene, not a premise the book can assume.

title: Making the Werewolf Frightening Again
body:
Familiar monsters are hard to scare with. The answer is not gore; it is procedure. A werewolf handled by a government department — containment protocols, disposal budgets, acronyms — becomes frightening because the institution has clearly done this before.

The horror of Blackout Moon is not the creature. It is the file.
